strengths: Novel application of test-time training (TTT) to streaming video understanding with well-motivated long-span prediction loss extending standard TTT formulations
Comprehensive system design combining TTTMEM layer, two-stage training, and modality-aware prompt-dependent memory reading that demonstrates strong empirical results
ELViM benchmark addresses an important unexplored evaluation scenario (episodic learning from long-past video experiences) with rigorous data pipeline preventing knowledge leakage

Extensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (Video-MME, LVBench, VideoEvalPro, StreamingBench) with thorough ablations clearly attributing performance gains; TTTMEM achieves comparable accuracy with 25% fewer tokens than merging
Consistent, substantial improvements especially on long-video understanding (14.2% on ELViM, 3-7% on standard benchmarks) and acceptable runtime overhead (0.1s per 3600 frames)
Clear presentation with effective architecture diagrams and detailed appendices; well-organized discussion of related work positioning contributions appropriately
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification for why a single gradient step per minibatch suffices for long-term consolidation across 3+ hour videos; connection between reconstruction and long-span prediction losses lacks formal rigor

Seemingly arbitrary hyperparameter choices: long-span prediction with T=2 predicts only ~24-32 frames despite 3-hour videos; appendix shows T=1-4 similar performance but no principled explanation for this range; chunk sizes and memory-reading parameters lack ablation

ELViM benchmark quality concerns: models achieve 98.7-99.3% accuracy on full videos (suggesting tasks may be easier than claimed), near-random 22.6% performance without video provides minimal signal, and modest scale (1849 questions, 1021 videos, 15 categories) with no inter-annotator agreement or human baselines

Incomplete architectural justification: audio tokens bypassing TTTMEM mentioned only in passing despite being significant simplification; deepstack embeddings excluded from TTTMEM in Appendix E due to computational cost, limiting mechanism expressiveness for Qwen3-VL's multi-stream design

Limited generalization analysis: all streaming evaluation at fixed 1 FPS without testing variable rates; no out-of-domain evaluation beyond tutorial/instructional videos; weak StreamingBench results (only 1.8% improvement) suggest possible overfit to long-video benchmarks

Reproducibility constraints: heavy dependence on Qwen3-VL backbone, ELViM generation via Gemini-2.5-Pro API, no reported random seeds or multiple runs; missing implementation details (θ initialization, exact gradient flow during TTTMEM)

strengths: Technically sound approach addressing a real problem in streaming video understanding with consistent empirical improvements (3-7% on long video benchmarks)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks with rigorous ablation studies examining different design choices
Novel application of test-time training (TTT) to streaming video memory, combined with a new long-span prediction objective
ELViM benchmark fills a genuine gap by evaluating whether models can learn procedural knowledge from past video experiences
Well-structured presentation with clear methodology and good visualization of the approach
All baselines implemented consistently using same backbone and training data, enabling fair comparison
weaknesses: Limited novelty—primarily a combinatorial application of existing techniques (TTT from Dalal et al. 2025, standard attention-based selection, token discarding). Individual components are not novel
Weak conceptual motivation for why TTT specifically helps long-term memory; fast-weight updates preserve information, but paper lacks deep analysis of what is actually stored and recoverable
Marginal improvements on StreamingBench (0.3-0.7%) where long-term memory is not critical, suggesting limited generalization beyond the specific evaluation setup

ELViM benchmark limitations: restricted to tutorial/procedural videos (limited domain generalization), relatively small (1,849 questions), merged videos average only 49 minutes (not fully testing claimed 3+ hour capability), heavy filtering using Gemini/Qwen may introduce bias
Very high computational requirements (32×H800 GPUs for 48+16 hours) severely limit reproducibility and practical adoption by most researchers
Evaluation limited to QA tasks only—no captioning, summarization, temporal localization, or human evaluation of response quality
Shallow analysis of model failures: only 3 qualitative examples provided; unclear when long-term memory helps least and which question types are problematic

Key design choices inadequately justified: T=2 for long-span prediction shows similar performance to T=1, T=4, T=16 (Table 10); no clear reason to discard rather than merge tokens despite claims; two-stage training appears necessitated by GPU constraints rather than principled design
Limited insight into what fast-weight parameters actually learn and potential overfitting to recent frames despite long-span regularization

strengths: Novel application of test-time training (TTT) to streaming video understanding with well-motivated long-span prediction objective for preserving long-term memory
Strong empirical results: 3-7% improvements on long video benchmarks and 14.2% on new ELViM benchmark, with robust scaling across different memory budgets and frame counts

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including thorough ablation studies, multiple benchmarks (Video-MME, LVBench, VideoEvalPro, StreamingBench), and detailed analysis of performance vs temporal distance

ELViM benchmark is a valuable contribution addressing a genuine gap—first benchmark explicitly designed to test learning and recall from episodic video memory with rigorous pipeline preventing knowledge leakage
Technically sound with practical considerations: maintains streaming constraints, minimal computational overhead (0.1s/frame, negligible FLOPs), constant GPU memory footprint
Extensive experimental documentation with detailed appendices supporting reproducibility (statistics, qualitative analysis, additional ablations, FLOP analysis)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is applying existing TTT (Sun et al., 2024; Dalal et al., 2025) with straightforward long-span prediction modification; lacks deeper analysis of why this approach works or what information is preserved in fast weights

Experimental fairness concerns: non-streaming baselines use 10 FPS with 16k tokens while streaming uses 1 FPS with 16k tokens, making direct comparison problematic; missing ablation where non-streaming also uses 1 FPS

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: no analysis of fast-weight information capacity compared to token-based approaches, no visualization of learned representations, limited analysis of how temporal information decays in W_t

ELViM benchmark limitations: moderate size (1849 questions), focused solely on procedural knowledge (generalization unclear), uses video merging rather than actual temporal gaps, lacks inter-annotator agreement metrics, potential dataset bias for post-mid-2025 videos
Training data separation concerns: LLaVA-Video-178k training data reportedly contains videos up to 3 hours; potential data leakage for similar-length sequences not clearly ruled out

Component contribution uncertainty: modality-aware memory reading adds only 0.2-3.1% improvement (Table 2) while adding complexity; unclear attribution of gains between TTT core, memory reading, and two-stage training
Architecture choices poorly justified: 2-layer MLP depth, 16 heads, T=2 prediction span chosen empirically without sensitivity analysis; chunk sizes appear arbitrary
Limited failure analysis: qualitative examples in Appendix C provide insufficient insight into when TTTMEM fails, what information is hardest to preserve, or behavior on adversarial sequences
Reproducibility gaps: complex two-stage training pipeline with multiple hyperparameters; ELViM dataset release plan unclear; implementation details scattered across main text and appendices
